title: From the Desi Aisle to the Frozen Mainstream: Indian Food Brands Storm American Grocery
excerpt: Samosas, naan and roti wraps once confined to specialty stores are now stocked in thousands of mainstream US supermarkets as Indian cuisine becomes America's fastest-rising flavor.
body:
There was a time when an Indian American craving a samosa or a fresh naan had exactly one option: drive to the nearest desi grocer, often a long trip across town. That monopoly is over. Indian food brands are pushing aggressively into mainstream American supermarkets, and the frozen and shelf-stable aisles of Kroger, Costco, Stop & Shop and Whole Foods are starting to look a lot more familiar to NRI shoppers.

## Context & Background

The backdrop is a structural shift in American eating. Indian food is now described as the **second-fastest-growing global cuisine in the US**, and the broader ethnic-food market is valued at roughly **$24.5 billion**. Retailers across natural, conventional and club channels report sustained demand for bold, authentic global flavors — and Indian brands, long stuck in the specialty niche, are racing to meet it.

Leading the charge is **Truly Indian**, a brand of the fourth-generation, family-owned ADF Foods, founded in India in 1932. Since launching in the US in May 2024, Truly Indian has expanded to more than 1,300 stores nationwide, selling handmade frozen samosas, low-glycemic tandoori naans, plant-based entrees, and "Indian Street Wraps" pitched as India's answer to the burrito. The company produces something on the order of 150,000 hand-stretched naans a day.

## Current Developments

The brand's momentum has only accelerated. Truly Indian was named a **2026 NEXTY Award finalist in two categories** — for its Tikka Masala Naan and a Crispy Chili Mango Chutney — at the Natural Products Expo, a marker of credibility in the mainstream natural-foods world. Its naans are billed as US category firsts: the only frozen naans formulated to be vegan, Non-GMO Project Verified, low-glycemic, Kosher and Halal.

Mainstream grocers are also building Indian food in-house. The beloved Texas chain **H-E-B** recently debuted its first-ever "Masala House" line at a new Irving location — house-made chicken masala, butter chicken, naan and chutney dips sold under the retailer's own banner. When a 400-store American chain decides Indian ready-meals deserve a private label, the cuisine has unambiguously crossed over. And the trend reaches beyond food: Indian jewelry giant Tanishq, having just entered the US, has publicly argued there is enormous room for other Indian retail brands in America.

## Diaspora Impact

For the diaspora, the convenience is transformative — and a little bittersweet. A frozen samosa from the corner Kroger will never match a mother's hand-folded version, but for time-strapped NRI families it is a genuine gift, putting a taste of home within arm's reach on any weeknight. It also validates a culture: seeing tandoori naan in the same freezer as pizza and dumplings tells second-generation kids that their food belongs on the American table, not in a separate, hidden aisle.

There is a quieter consequence too. As mainstream chains and big CPG players move in, the independent desi grocery stores that anchored immigrant neighborhoods for decades face new competition. The community hub that doubled as a cultural lifeline may have to evolve to survive.

Analysts see the category's growth as durable rather than faddish. Indian cuisine's appeal to American shoppers rests on the same pillars driving the paneer and plant-protein booms: bold flavor, vegetarian-friendly options, and a halo of perceived healthfulness around spices like turmeric and ingredients like lentils and chickpeas. As distribution widens from the coastal metros into the heartland, brands are betting that a butter-chicken bowl or a frozen samosa can become as unremarkable on an American grocery list as a frozen pizza — a normalization that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago.

## What's Next

Expect the land grab to intensify, with tariff pressures and supply-chain costs testing margins even as demand climbs. More private-label Indian lines from major grocers are likely, alongside expanded distribution for brands like Truly Indian into club and conventional channels. The frozen aisle has become the new frontier of Indian food in America — and for the diaspora, the sight of a familiar samosa under fluorescent supermarket lights is proof that desi flavor has gone fully mainstream.
